title: How does a stranger get from download to a running hub?
lead: Pick how the desktop app installs. I recommend A: one installer of about 120-150 MB that carries the hub, Node and Claude Code inside it, so a stranger downloads, clicks through, pastes an API key and is running. Confidence: medium-high on the approach, medium on the size.
for_you: Strangers skip Node, git and the terminal; a first-run screen asks for the API key and project folders

for_you.text: Builds run on your PC as today; updates reach users through the app's own signed updater on GitHub Releases
Amends decisions 4 and 49: the app still attaches and Quit still leaves the hub running, but the hub now lives in the app folder. Your own clone keeps working through hubDir

context: Today the desktop app (decision 49, release v0.1.0) is only a window on a hub the user installs by hand: Node, clone, npm install, login, start. Matt: 'why would we go through the trouble of making a Tauri wrapper if people had to do 400 steps?' install-research (memo M030) compared four routes. Licence: Anthropic's terms allow shipping Claude Code inside a product if the binary is unmodified, users bring their own key or subscription and usage is never resold; the Agent SDK is all rights reserved, so it goes in the installer, never in the public repo (Claude's reading, not legal advice). A single-exe build (Node SEA, bun) was ruled out: same size, experimental, needs a bundler. winget can be a second channel later.

options.name: Everything in one installer
options.summary: The installer carries node.exe, the hub, crux scripts and its packages including Claude Code, as plain files. The app starts that hub detached, exactly as now. First-run screen for the key and folders. Updates through the Tauri updater.
pros: One download, nothing else to install, works offline after install
Fewest ways to fail on a stranger's PC
cons: 120-150 MB download, and each update re-downloads it all
Anthropic's closed-source parts ship inside our installer (allowed under their terms, as read)
options.effort: Medium: bundling step, first-run screen, updater, an installer hook that stops the hub before an update

options.name: Small installer that fetches the rest
options.summary: A ~10 MB installer; on first run the app downloads Node and the hub's packages, then shows the same key and folder screen.
pros: Small download; Anthropic's parts come straight from npm, the cleanest licence position
Updates of the hub can be small
cons: More ways to fail: firewalls, proxies, npm outages, half-finished first runs
Needs the network on first run
options.effort: Medium to large: a download-and-repair flow with progress and retry

options.name: Keep the window only
options.summary: Leave the app as it is: users set up the hub by hand from the README, then install the app.
cons: Strangers still face Node, git and a terminal, which is what Matt objected to

recommendation: A is the only option that matches 'download, click, paste a key'. The size is the price, and an installer that works offline is easier to support than a first-run download that can break halfway. B stays the fallback if the size or the licence reading becomes a problem.
change_mind: If Anthropic's terms are read more strictly, or 150 MB proves a barrier, go B.

settles.value: one installer carrying Node, the hub and its packages; app still attaches to the hub and Quit leaves it running; updates via the signed Tauri updater on GitHub Releases
